Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 23, 2026

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tomorrow marks the Full Moon, but tonight's Moon already looks almost full.
  • 23, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 97% of its surface visible.
  • If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Tranquillitatis and Fecunditatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tomorrow marks the Full Moon, but tonight's Moon already looks almost full. It's still technically in its Waxing Gibbous phase, with just a small portion of its surface left in the darkness.

As of Monday, Nov. 23, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 97% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Tranquillitatis and Fecunditatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau. With binoculars, you'll also see the Grimaldi Basin, the Endymion Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 15, and 16 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

Recent findings suggest that according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a Latest Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • is investigating Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton stated, as a report identified one of her associates as a key decision-maker at the Singapore-based company.
  • Clayton stated the investigation was "ongoing" on Sunday, the day before Nvidia revealed it had reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a position he resigned from in part because of his relationship with Alice Huang.
  • Industry observers note that alice Huang was a key figure in Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton stated, as a report identified one of her associates as a key decision-maker at the Singapore-based company.

Clayton stated the investigation was "ongoing" on Sunday, the day before Nvidia revealed it had reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a position he resigned from in part because of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Industry observers note that alice Huang was a key figure in Megaspeed International, a cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia. U.S. intelligence reportedly believes she is a Chinese spy.

"There is an investigation ongoing into her firm and into her," Clayton told ABC on Sunday, adding that, "Nvidia chips, they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants, that's why we're focusing on this.".

Nvidia's board revealed Jensen Huang's return before the opening bell on Monday, saying it had "a series of discussions and meetings" with him.

It added that it received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is confident that his reinstatement "poses no national security risk.".

Alice Huang's associate, Chinese national Li Ming, who is now out on bail in Singapore, was "deeply involved" in Megaspeed's activities and took part in major decisions, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Saturday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The Singapore charges against Li concern alleged false representations to Super Micro Computer, a U.S.-based firm with known links to chipmaker Nvidia, though Megaspeed is not named in those charges.

Last week, the Commerce and Justice departments said that the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over potential export-control violations. Their joint statement said Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security and Singapore law enforcement interviewed Huang during an on-site check in June 2025.

The Justice Department later took the lead in the criminal investigation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CBS on Sunday that the administration was seeking answers from Nvidia about its chip sales to China, including who oversaw compliance and which levels of the tech giant knew about the activity.

According to recent reports, separately, The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang was in contact with an officer of a top Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 through fall 2026, citing people briefed on U.S. intelligence reports.

Bloomberg reported last week that the Justice Department is investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang helped smuggle Super Micro products to China.

Li faces five charges in Singapore, including two counts of fraud by false representation, along with allegations involving the operation of a firm he controlled, unauthorized bank-account access and another company director's duties.

Prosecutors allege he falsely told Super Micro that the company would hold and lease the servers it purchased.

It has been revealed that the Journal reported that Li is out on bail and that his case is ongoing. He was offered bail of S$1 million in March 2025. The Singapore charges do not name Megaspeed.

Earlier this month, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs remarked that police had found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang committed offenses related to the possible inaccurate declarations under investigation.

The ministry stated she was issued a stern warning for providing information that police assessed as knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role at Megaspeed. It also said Singapore had not investigated her for espionage.

Megaspeed has stated it is a "legitimate and lawful business" and that Huang left the firm in August 2025.

Industry observers note that the scrutiny is set to intensify in Washington. Jensen Huang and the company's general counsel, Tim Teter, have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2, respectively.

The committees mentioned they want answers about Nvidia's role in allowing Chinese actors to access advanced chips and the involvement of a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

Recent findings suggest that speaking to CNBC's Squawk Box on Sunday U.S. time, Ryan Fedasiuk, a former advisor for U.S.-China Bilateral Affairs at the State Department, remarked that there was "still a lot we don't know" about the case.

He said lawmakers would likely focus on Nvidia's customer relationships and "who knew what at the company when.".

According to recent reports, fedasiuk added that there was "a very good chance" investigators would find that people at Nvidia knew their products could be used for restricted purposes. He characterized the existing evidence as containing "multiple" smoking guns.

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

In a recent development, there are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An key note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

GTA 6 lets you use social media to find robbery targets

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) has been out for less than a week, but players have already found a plethora of considered details in the massive sandbox game.
  • Sources indicate that snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, filled with photos and memes reflecting the game's satirical rendition of the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that as such, GTA 6 players have discovered that Snapmatic can be used to identify robbery targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) has been out for less than a week, but players have already found a plethora of considered details in the massive sandbox game. Among them is a novel method players are using to get more money in GTA 6, helping them find robbery targets that are worth their time. It also doubles as an key reminder about internet safety.

Sources indicate that snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, filled with photos and memes reflecting the game's satirical rendition of the U.S. This includes people showing off drugs, cars, and weapons in a bid for clout. Like Instagram, Snapmatic also allows its fictional customers to tag a location in their posts.

Sources indicate that as such, GTA 6 players have discovered that Snapmatic can be used to identify robbery targets. Simply find a post with a location tagged, and open the menu you'd use to like it or view comments. Under the "Like" option will be "Set Destination," which will mark the location of the Snapmatic post on your map. You can then head there to relieve characters of their belongings (typically via the use of notable violence).

It's an interesting gameplay mechanic that also serves as a reminder to be careful about what you post online. While the world of GTA 6 is a heightened version of reality, it does still have some basis in truth. There have been multiple real-life instances of criminals finding their victims via social media posts, something that's been occurring for years.

Last month, a UK man was convicted of stealing £48,000 (about $62,900) and various items from a home after seeing the family's social media posts indicating they'd be out hosting a Chinese Newly introduced Year celebration. In 2021, four people were arrested in Italy for allegedly stealing from celebrities and influencers after monitoring their Instagram accounts, reportedly using victims' posts to identify tagged locations, entry points, and when they'd be away from home. Back in 2016, a California man was convicted of stealing personal items from female college students after finding them via GPS locations in photos posted to Instagram.

Even if you exclude location tags and don't mention your movements in your posts, you can still be vulnerable. Late last year, four French men travelled to Australia in order to rob a home of items reportedly valued at around $AU10 million ($6.6 million). According to court documents, the thieves saw photos of luxury goods that a victim had posted to Instagram, as well as images of their backyard and local surroundings. The thieves then used ChatGPT to search for where these pictures were taken, narrowing it down to a specific Australian city and suburb, which helped them locate the house.

Using social media to pick robbery targets in GTA 6 won't attract the same legal consequences and prison time that it would in real life. Rather, it serves as a neat little trick to help ambitious, self-starting criminals find worthwhile heists. However, this mechanic should also serve as an important reminder about the dangers of real-life Insta-bragging, and a warning to be careful about what you share online.   • In-game social media app Snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, offering a scrollable feed of posts from fictional characters showing off their very lootable possessions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) offers a satirical rendition of the U.S., filled with cars, crime, and shenanigans worthy of the game's Florida-inspired setting. It also incorporates many digital elements of modern life, including social media. Of course, where there's social media, there are inevitably memes.

In-game social media app Snapmatic is GTA 6's version of Instagram, offering a scrollable feed of posts from fictional characters showing off their very lootable possessions. However, Snapmatic isn't just filled with posts sharing potential theft coordinates. It also contains a plethora of memes specifically created to populate GTA 6's social media.

Players promptly took note of GTA 6's memes, praising them for accurately capturing the irreverent vibe and frequently off-colour humour that typically characterises such media.

Recent findings suggest that "GTA 6 is so realistic that I thought this was a real meme," posted X user @thisdopenose, sharing an image of an in-game meme. In the meme, the text "bisexuals when they realise you can have sex more than twice" is edited onto a monochrome image of a man crying. The popular post has 94,000 likes at time of writing.

"They need to give a pay rise to whoever came up with the shitposts on Snapmatic bro these things are so funny," wrote @vandalfeet.

Some of GTA 6's in-game memes even referred to memes about GTA 6 itself. It's been 13 years since GTA 5 released, with many fans having eagerly awaited the franchises' latest instalment for over a decade. In the interim, it became a common meme for people to jokingly express disbelief that various other events had occurred "before GTA 6" arrived.

Developer Rockstar Games appears to have been aware of such memes, creating its own versions referring to GTA 6's fictional video game Race and Chase 7. ("Race'n'Chase" was the original working title for the first Grand Theft Auto game released in 1997).

Rockstar Games had teams dedicated to creating in-game media, aiming to flesh out GTA 6's world and make it feel more immersive. Judging by fans' reactions, it appears to have paid off. Parent company Take-Two Interactive estimates that GTA 6 achieved $3.79 billion in sales on day one alone, making it one of the biggest entertainment media launches ever. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's a commonly asked question about everyone's favorite spicy hookup site, AdultFriendFinder: Is AFF safe to use?
  • To better understand the risks of using AdultFriendFinder, we consulted Anna Larkina, a Web Data and Privacy Analysis Expert at Kaspersky, one of the world's leading cybersecurity services, to ask about the kinds of threats people might face on AFF and how they can mitigate those risks.
  • To begin, it's worth remembering that there's a risk inherent to using any online service, whether it's an adult dating site or otherwise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's a commonly asked question about everyone's favorite spicy hookup site, AdultFriendFinder: Is AFF safe to use? We get it. It's nerve-wracking when things get very NSFW. Unlike other well-known dating sites, the AFF interface is full of adult content. To the untrained eye, AFF looks like a hotbed of would-be scammers. It's perfectly reasonable to question its legitimacy. AFF customers want some fun, but they also want to be safe.

To better understand the risks of using AdultFriendFinder, we consulted Anna Larkina, a Web Data and Privacy Analysis Expert at Kaspersky, one of the world's leading cybersecurity services, to ask about the kinds of threats people might face on AFF and how they can mitigate those risks.

To begin, it's worth remembering that there's a risk inherent to using any online service, whether it's an adult dating site or otherwise. Even the most reputable websites have been exploited and experienced major hacks over the years. “Users should remember that any service can potentially encounter various cybersecurity issues,” Larkina told us. That includes “data leaks, attacks on third-party contractors, or issues related to the human factor.”  The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

But the risks are, of course, higher on certain websites. With a regular merchant website, for instance, you’re only handing over your credit card information (which is very valuable, admittedly), but with a dating site, you’re potentially providing your credit card details plus crucial personal information, from your date of birth and nationality to your address and phone number. That kind of information can heighten the risk — it's very valuable to online scammers who seek to steal it for use or resale.

While this is a risk you take with literally any dating service, AdultFriendFinder is perhaps more vulnerable than most dating sites because of the nature of its content and user base. It’s important to understand any potential security problems.

While NSFW content is permitted on AFF — it's actually encouraged — users are under no obligation to post nude photos of themselves, or get down and dirty on a webcam feed. Many users opt to do so, of course, and while there's no judgment here — let that freak flag fly high and proud, we say — you do risk potentially awkward conversations with family, friends, or co-workers if they happen to stumble across your account. (That would mean they'd have to fess up to being AFF users too, but even so...).

Unfortunately, bad actors can exploit and use your own personal information against you.

According to recent reports, “Data from services with adult content or dating services can be especially sensitive for owners, because it’s more personal,” warns Larkina. “If fraudsters somehow obtain such private data, they can use it for more ‘efficient’ blackmailing or targeted phishing.” Needless to say, you should be wary of how you use the site and what information you share, especially if you have a public-facing job.

Sources indicate that while dating sites now invest heavily in cybersecurity protections, online threats are constant and keep evolving. Hackers eager to discover treasure troves of personal and financial information often target online dating platforms, which can make users feel super vulnerable.

According to recent reports, adultFriendFinder has suffered two major security breaches, which is actually a pretty stellar record of security over its entire 30-year history. In 2016, hackers gained access to the personal information of four million AFF owners before the breach was found and stopped. And a larger breach occurred in 2016, affecting some 300 million AFF accounts, including 15 million that had been officially deleted by users but whose data had not been properly expunged from the AFF servers.

To combat phishing, AFF offers the option to verify your identity with government-issued identification. This verification process is still optional — it's not required when setting up an account. We recommend doing it and setting a search filter to verified accounts only. That way you'll only interact with people who are 100% legit. It's a surefire way to protect yourself against scammers.

While the private information you give AFF (your real name and email address, for example) isn't public-facing, AFF’s dating profiles are public by default, so if you include a picture of your face (as many accounts do), you can be recognized by friends, co-workers, and family members.

And since AFF has suffered two major hacks before, there’s always a chance it could happen again, which could result in your email address and information ending up in a dodgy database.

Does this all mean you should never use AdultFriendFinder, or any dating site? Absolutely not. We're here to help you protect yourself and stay vigilant, not to discourage you from signing up.

Larkina has shared an additional list of best practices to help you mitigate risks while having fun on AFF or any other dating site:.

To protect your accounts, use strong and unique passwords, change them regularly, and if possible, enable two-factor authentication.

Be extremely cautious with what you share with strangers, especially when it comes to sensitive information or intimate photos. “Always assess reputational and other risks before posting or sending anything,” cautions Larkina.

When using AFF in particular, limit your interactions to users who have verified their identity.

According to recent reports, summing up her advice, Larkina urges online dating service users to treat these “platforms as public spaces, not as private ones” as far as possible, and be ever mindful that “every piece of data you provide — email, phone number, username, etc. — becomes part of your digital footprint.” If you’re careful about what you share and who you share it with, you can safely enjoy AdultFriendFinder and any other dating site.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto VI was released on consoles last week, with millions of players exploring Leonida on Xbox and PS5 consoles. But one major question remains: What's happening with the online mode?

According to recent reports, the GTA Online component of Grand Theft Auto V has kept that 13-year-old game relevant across three console generations, with a recent leak suggesting Rockstar makes as much as $500 million annually from microtransactions alone. One would think that means GTA VI will have a similar online offering available at launch, but that isn't the case. Per a Rockstar statement given to IGN, as well as all available marketing language on digital storefronts, GTA VI is a "single-player experience.".

There was no online component at launch, nor has Rockstar announced any intention of adding one after launch. Sadly, that is all the concrete information anyone can provide right now.

However, that doesn't mean all hope is lost. It's worth remembering that both GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2 introduced as solo experiences and got online modes later, though it was only a matter of months in both cases. Given that Rockstar hasn't even said if there will be a upcoming GTA Online experience for VI, it's probably safe to assume the wait will be longer this time.

Sources indicate that the fact that the existing GTA Online is so wildly successful (with no signs of slowing down) means Rockstar isn't necessarily incentivized to make a new one right away. It also means Rockstar has to decide if it wants to keep two different GTA Online experiences running at the same time, should GTA VI ever get one. As IGN noted, Grand Theft Auto publisher Take-Two currently supports two different NBA 2K Online games in the Asian market; the first rolled out in 2012 and its sequel in 2017, but they're both popular enough to coexist to this day.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, we don't have a definitive answer on when we'll get a newly introduced GTA Online mode tied to the new game, but hey, single-player games aren't so bad. I'm sure there will be plenty of hours of entertainment to be had in GTA VI as it is.

Industry News: GTA 6 on PC revision: What we know about when it releases

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles at launch (it will also be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming, with limits).
  • It has been revealed that GTA 6 has no confirmed PC release date.
  • An October 2026 report from gaming business media site Gamesbeat reveals a potential PC launch in early 2027, which is sooner than we expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles at launch (it will also be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming, with limits).

It has been revealed that GTA 6 has no confirmed PC release date. Given Rockstar's history with PC ports, we originally thought gamers were in for a long wait.

An October 2026 report from gaming business media site Gamesbeat reveals a potential PC launch in early 2027, which is sooner than we expected.

Grand Theft Auto VI arrived on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on Nov. 19, 2026, but PC players will have to wait a while longer. Rockstar has confirmed that the game will not be available for PC gamers at launch, and no PC version has been officially announced yet.

Recent findings suggest that despite that, we recently got some good news: GamesBeat reports that GTA 6 will get a PC release sometime in Q1 of 2027. GamesBeat has a good track record with unannounced news like this. According to their reporting, the GTA 6 PC release window was confirmed by industry sources familiar with Rockstar's plans. They spoke with the outlet under the condition of anonymity.

Rockstar and Take-Two haven't given an official reason for skipping PC at launch, but a few factors are typically cited when publishers stagger releases this way.

Console hardware is standardized, which tends to make optimization more straightforward than building for the huge range of PC configurations. Some industry data has also indicated that consoles generate higher per-unit revenue, giving publishers an incentive to front-load console sales.

It has been revealed that A more cynical take is that Take-Two could just be double-dipping, hoping fans who can't wait for the PC launch will buy the console first, then buy the PC version later. A PC Gamer poll found that 39 percent of respondents stated they're fine waiting for a port rather than needing it on day one, suggesting a meaningful share of the PC audience isn't treating the delay as a dealbreaker.

However, there could be another, less financially motivated reason for all of this.

Speaking to YouTuber KiwiTalkz, former Rockstar producer John Ricchio explained that building for consoles first and scaling up to PC is technically easier than the reverse, since consoles have fixed, predictable hardware. According to IGN, Ricchio stated it's simpler to start with tighter constraints and add polish later than to build a PC-first game and then try to trim it down to fit console limitations.

Without an official release date, gamers have had to speculate on the most likely launch window for a GTA 6 PC version.

If you look at several past Rockstar games, you can see that there's typically a significant amount of time between the console launch and the PC port.

Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto 4 was released in April 2008 and didn't reach PC's until December. Grand Theft Auto V was released in Sept. 2013, and its PC counterpart was released 19 months later in April 2015. Red Dead Redemption 2 arrived on PC roughly a year after its console release.

Industry observers note that the one exception was Grand Theft Auto: The Trilogy – The Definitive Edition, which introduced simultaneously across platforms in 2021. Based on that track record, a GTA 6 PC port, if it follows the usual pattern, could be a year or more away.

A report from The Verge claimed that Xbox would have exclusive rights to stream GTA 6 via its cloud gaming service at launch, a claim that was recently confirmed. The report noted that PC gamers would be able to play GTA 6 on day one, despite Rockstar's lack of news about a potential release window for a PC port. Unfortunately, Xbox Gaming's Chief Strategy Officer, Matthew Ball, shot down this report. Ball wrote on his personal X account that The Verge's coverage led to some "misreporting.".

Again, the game will be available to play on Xbox consoles via Xbox Cloud Gaming, but that service faces strict monthly limits, which will make it difficult to play through the game in a timely fashion.

Fortunately, a GamesBeat report suggests gamers may not have to wait a full year for a PC release, though it remains unconfirmed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI has been out for less than a week, but there are already a whole host of tips, tricks and memes out there.

Rumors, too. One that we've seen repeated and reshared recently is a rumor about GTA 6's online multiplayer version, and the criteria players will supposedly need to meet in order to play it.

Recent findings suggest that "Rockstar Games has reportedly confirmed that players will be required to achieve 100% single-player story completion—including all stranger missions and collectibles—before being granted access to 'GTA 6 Online' servers at launch," posted Chaos Crave on X. At the time of writing that's had around 1,400 shares, and we've seen the claim being repeated by other accounts.

The problem? It's not true. As the Community Note attached to the post points out, Chaos Crave (per its own bio) is a "Satirical News account".

Rockstar Games has confirmed no such thing — and in fact, we don't even know when an online GTA 6 will be available, let alone any other details.

Recent findings suggest that will an online mode for GTA 6 be coming at some point? Probably, given how much money it makes for Rockstar. But for now, we'll just have to keep exploring the single player world.

Industry News: ‘Worst COP ever’: Climate talks collapse after draft deal fails to include fossil fuels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Negotiations at the United Nations' climate summit collapsed on Sunday as the U.K., EU and others rejected a draft deal that failed to include fossil fuels.
  • Since the U.N.'s Climate Change Conference — or COP31 — began in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov.
  • Antonio Guterres, the U.N.'s secretary-general, said he was "deeply disappointed" that no consensus was reached.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Negotiations at the United Nations' climate summit collapsed on Sunday as the U.K., EU and others rejected a draft deal that failed to include fossil fuels.

Since the U.N.'s Climate Change Conference — or COP31 — began in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9, almost 200 countries have been locked in talks to reach a "cover decision," with a number of drafts issued in recent days.

Antonio Guterres, the U.N.'s secretary-general, said he was "deeply disappointed" that no consensus was reached.

Talks centered on electrification, funding for developing nations and ways to respond to scientific warnings about rising global temperatures, with the 1.5 degrees Celsius target likely to be overshot.

But on Sunday, after negotiations overran by almost two days, the latest cover proposal made no mention of fossil fuels, prompting outcry from governments and campaigners.

Recent findings suggest that speaking on behalf of the EU, Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien said the conference was "hijacked by some oil states," when asked by Reuters about Saudi Arabia's role in the negotiations. CNBC has contacted Saudi Arabia for comment.

The EU said it rejected the deal because the text "does not respond to the science" of climate change. "We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels," it said in a statement Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that the U.K. government "does not believe the cover decision proposed by the Presidencies meets the moment," it remarked on Sunday. "It moves us backwards on the science when we must accelerate implementation," it said.

Representatives of island nations — vulnerable to the effects of climate change — refused to sign the draft text. "Three years ago in Dubai, the nations of the world agreed by consensus to transition away from fossil fuels in their energy systems," Philip Davis, prime minister of the Bahamas, mentioned in an online statement, referring to the UAE Consensus made at COP28 in 2023.

Recent findings suggest that "Small island states produce less than 1% of global emissions, yet we carry the weight of a crisis we did not cause. We have brought prepares, commitments and patience to three decades of these talks. Antalya exhausted that patience," Davis noted.

Albert Salamanca, a senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute Asia, told CNBC via email that the lack of consensus on a deal is "tantamount to a death sentence for vulnerable communities still unable to respond in a timely manner to emerging risks.".

Industry observers note that developing nations are facing "abandonment," according to Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank Power Shift Africa. He described the event as "the worst COP ever" in an online statement, adding that "rich countries blocked the creation of a just transition mechanism.".

The World Wildlife Fund, or WWF, described the lack of progress on finance for developing nations as having "real-world consequences for the lives and livelihoods of the planet's most vulnerable communities," in an online statement.

Nonsikelelo Nkomo-Mabobe, business development manager at Solidaridad, an organization that promotes fair supply chains, welcomed some of the language in COP31's proposed Antalya Pact, with "promising signs around food security, which is acknowledged as heavily affected by climate impacts." But she remarked a finance gap remains.

"Funding must be easier for frontline communities to access, and it must be traceable once it has been disbursed," Nkomo-Mabobe mentioned in an email to CNBC.

The WWF welcomed the engagement from participants of the COP31 Action Agenda, which comprises of businesses and other non-governmental organizations. "Momentum from communities, cities and businesses is real despite what happened in the negotiating rooms," it mentioned.

A major goal of COP31 was to increase global electrification to 35% by 2035 — up from 23% today, with a Global Climate Action Agenda Electrification Delivery Package declared on Thursday as a "first milestone" to achieve this.

Recent findings suggest that the U.N.'s Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said on Sunday that "around half" the global economy is accelerating electrification, adding that the package had made "real economy" progress. More than 90 countries signed the pledge, according to Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations.

"Frustratingly," the pledge does not detail how the electricity will be generated, according to Ellen Dorsey, executive director of the Wallace Global Fund — around 57% of electricity was generated by fossil fuels in 2025, according to think tank Ember.

In a recent development, dorsey urged states to provide electricity to those in developing countries. "Will we ensure governments provide electricity to hundreds of millions who lack it, by leapfrogging fossil fuels build-out and instead invest in small-scale renewables?" she stated in an email to CNBC.

According to recent reports, preserving sea life has "often been overlooked" in climate negotiations, according to the U.N. The language referring to oceans in the draft cover decision was "slightly weakened," according to Nicolas Entrup, director of international relations at marine conservation organization OceanCare, in an email to CNBC. But he said he was hopeful that the Antalya Ocean Current, a U.N. blueprint to hold future talks on oceans and climate change, would be carried forward.

Recent findings suggest that more than 95% of island and coastal nations now have ocean preservation in their climate intends, but around 60% of those commitments rely on external funding, according to research by ocean conservancy groups. Scientists also called for ongoing investment to monitor oceans beyond short-term research.

Sources indicate that "I share the deep disappointment of many: COP31 has been unable to agree on concerns related to both Presidency's led decisions," Stiell said. Turkey and Australia shared the presidency at this year's conference.

- CNBC's Sawdah Bhaimiya contributed to this report.

Clarification: This story has been updated to more accurately reflect Nicolas Entrup's comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an open letter to the CEOs of Amazon and eBay, a coalition of 155 child advocacy groups called on the online marketplaces to stop selling toys powered by artificial intelligence.

The letter argues that AI toys are "cheap, easy to buy, and largely untested." It lists numerous risks associated with the products, including sexually explicit content, unproven educational claims, privacy violations, and instructions for how to access and use harmful household items.

Recent findings suggest that the letter's publication follows the release of annual toy research conducted by U.S. PIRG. While some AI products made important safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

Industry observers note that amazon subsequently removed the bunny and another toy capable of sexual exchanges from its platform. The letter identified over 50 AI toys available for sale on Amazon's U.S. marketplace.

"These products should be shown to be safe before they reach children, not withdrawn one at a time after harm is found," the letter said.

The effort was led by the child advocacy groups Fairplay, Alliance 4 Children CIC, and Set@16. eBay responded to the open letter in response to Mashable's request for comment.

"We are committed to protecting the buyers and sellers on our marketplace and we continually evaluate our policies and engage with regulators to ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards," an eBay spokesperson noted in an email.

Amazon told Mashable that it requires all products sold by third-parties to comply with applicable laws and regulations.

It has been revealed that "Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," the organization remarked in an email. "We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops.".

The letter notes that California banned toys with companion chatbots for children younger than 16, beginning Jan. 2027. A bill introduced in Congress would also ban AI chatbots in toys.

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk.

The Monday mood is positive after a nightmare week on Wall Street.

The bounce back across the major markets has gained steam throughout the premarket session, despite a rough handover from Asia.

A decent rebound for U.S. stocks looks set to help major markets crawl away from correction territory.

Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average are up over 1.5%, while the S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq-100 futures look set to outperform.

It follows a widely divergent handover from Asia and Europe. Technology stocks sank in overnight trading, with SK Hynix among the biggest losers, weighing on South Korea's Kospi.

But in Europe, tech rallied in early trade, pushing the Europe Stoxx 600 into the green.

Sources indicate that on Friday, the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite lost its gain for the year and the more concentrated Nasdaq-100 entered bear market territory on an intraday basis.

Anthropic is higher in premarket trading on Monday, following an 8.5% drop on Friday.

CrowdStrike shares are down over 7% in early trading, after it announced a $43.9 billion deal to buy Zscaler. Shares in the cloud security tech giant are up over 15% in premarket trading.

Meanwhile, chip stocks are also in the green, rebounding from last week's sell-off.

Nvidia remains in the eye of the storm. Shares are higher in premarket trading, after falling around 14% on Friday.

Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton, says there is an investigation into Alice Huang and her former manufacturer, Megaspeed. This comes amid reports that an associate of hers was a key decision-maker at the company.

Americans should brace themselves for more outage-related disruptions.

Jay Clayton stated on CNN's "State of the Union" that outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their systems to adapt to the AI age.

CNBC's Alex Harring reports that the tech outages are fueling a upcoming doomsday economy.

CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.

This festive season could be marked by a upcoming tradition — agentic holiday shopping.

Newly introduced Salesforce research suggests shoppers are more comfortable using AI to research products and get recommendations than handing an agent the ability to pay: roughly three-quarters say they trust AI recommendations, while only 9% of personal agent users say they've shared financial information to make purchases.

Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens.

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

— CNBC's John Melloy, Shikhar Gupta, Jordan Novet, Garrett Downs, Alex Harring, Kai Nicol-Schwarz and Hugh Son contributed to this report.

Recent findings suggest that if the barista at your neighborhood coffee shop knows your order before you even walk up to the counter, it might be time to consider learning to make that double Americano at home. With today being National Espresso Day and no shortage of espresso machines on sale ahead of Black Friday, that opportunity is particularly apt.

Industry observers note that each deal below is for a machine that a WIRED reviewer has tested and vetted in their own kitchen. If you take advantage of the savings now, your machine may arrive in time for Thanksgiving, allowing you to impress everyone with your post-dinner cappuccino-making skills.

For more deals, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals, as well as early deals at Amazon and Home Depot.

Updated November 23: I’ve added fresh deals on machines from Diletta, Fellow, and De'Longhi, plus some accessories. I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

WIRED reviewers have tried and liked a couple of machines from Diletta, a line of Italian-made, classic semiautomatics exclusive to Seattle Coffee Gear, and they’re all on sale today through December 14.

Industry observers note that we reviewed the Bello+ in 2024, appreciating the stylish, industrial design (handmade in Milan) and easily maneuverable steam wand. Our reviewer found it a bit finicky, but Seattle Coffee Gear indicates it does have a programmable pre-infusion for repeatable recipes.

Best Traditional Espresso Machine in our guide to the best, the Mio is stylish and built to last, with an analog design and a two-year warranty. It also makes for a solid first “real” espresso machine with its built-in shot timer and pressure gauge.

Fellow set some pretty lofty expectations with the release of its sleek Aiden coffee maker in 2024, and according to former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage, the brand didn't disappoint on its first attempt at an espresso machine. The ability to adjust flow rates and pressure curves was once the province of, as Korfhage put it, only the “richest and nerdiest of nerds.” But Fellow now allows you—yes, you, at home in your kitchen—to fine-tune how water moves through the grounds, unlocking previously unforeseen dimensions of flavor.

According to recent reports, when we tested this machine, we liked it for a variety of reasons, including an easy-to-use milk frother and two swappable bean hoppers, which are especially helpful if you like to switch to decaf in the afternoons. It comes in a variety of finishes, but note that Beige is the cheapest of all right now, at only $915.

Sources indicate that this flashy, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing,” according to Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person. It has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the 2nd Gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a new portafilter.

Formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried, with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was easy enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos; I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.

The Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso. The Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and upcoming finishes, including this white one, a matte black-and-gold, and a sort of gunmetal gray.

In a recent development, we appreciated this semiautomatic’s slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. The cold-brew setting is more of a gimmick than a way to make actual cold brew, and some design choices are a bit quirky. Even so, it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.

Ninja sometimes has a reputation for doing too much, but we liked this semiautomatic as a beginner-friendly option that pulls some solid shots. It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, it also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for those features alone.

Industry observers note that former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested Terra Kaffe's newer Demi and noted it was perhaps the “dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee,” with just a dial and a button. Right now it's $200 off, or $300 off with a coffee subscription (Terra-Kaffe offers a house blend specifically made for use on its machines). Its bigger sibling, the TK-02, impressed our tester with its convenience, ease of use, front-facing water filter, and milk carafe. Though it didn't come out on top during a blind espresso taste test we did earlier this year, it's still a great-looking machine that's easy to use and is a whopping $400 off (or $500 with a coffee subscription) for Black Friday.

Atlas (3-month Gift subscription).

Atlas (6-month Gift subscription).

Maybe you or your recipient already has an espresso machine; in that case, they’ll need some quality beans. Our favorite coffee subscription, Atlas Coffee Club, has a upcoming gift option on offer for Black Friday: a quarterly subscription of three bags of unique, globally sourced coffee every three months for $59. You can choose any roast you want, including espresso roast and even Nespresso pods. If you’d rather buy an ongoing subscription for yourself, your first bag is free with Atlas’ Black Friday sale.

Former barista and WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell likes this little scale that includes three magnetic add-ons: a platform, a metal dosing cup, and a catch cup that fits directly onto almost any portafilter.

If grounds are sticking to the plastic components of your coffee grinder, Cottell recommends adding this durable, stylish spray bottle to your espresso setup.

Cottell likes situating this mat underneath your espresso setup, as the lip contains spills and the textured portion is great for drying tools post-washing.

According to recent reports, some machines come with a tamper; others don't. If yours doesn’t, Cottell recommends you get this one. The spring-loaded base unloads 15 pounds of force to create a perfectly flat puck inside your portafilter. (A click lets you know when to stop pushing, so it’s great for beginners, too.).

Tech Report: I cant stop making lunch with this German sandwich simulator

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The art of making a sandwich has been revered since John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, was so engrossed in a game of cards in 1762 he demanded meat between slices of bread to fuel his playing — it was a deeply espresso martini-coded move which saw all of his jealous mates also ask for one.
  • Over 250 years later, the subtle craft of 'wich is championed once again in an online sandwich-making simulator that threatens to eat into my GTA 6 time.
  • Created by German developer Gregor Weichbrodt with music by Scott Hühnerkrisp, a newly introduced sandwich simulator is exactly that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The art of making a sandwich has been revered since John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, was so engrossed in a game of cards in 1762 he demanded meat between slices of bread to fuel his playing — it was a deeply espresso martini-coded move which saw all of his jealous mates also ask for one.

Over 250 years later, the subtle craft of 'wich is championed once again in an online sandwich-making simulator that threatens to eat into my GTA 6 time.

Created by German developer Gregor Weichbrodt with music by Scott Hühnerkrisp, a newly introduced sandwich simulator is exactly that. "You make a sandwich. That's all," reads the simulator's about page. Notably, it's not the same as FiftyEight Studios' 2026 game Sandwich Simulator or Sandwich Squad's 2024 Sandwich Sim.

Each sandwich gets a serial number and a permalink, so you can revisit your creation later for reasons I can't quite conjure here beyond lunch inspo. To date, 42,375 unique sandwiches have been made on the simulator since it released in Oct. 2026. For example, my tower of power sandwich will probably live on the internet after I shuffle off this mortal coil.

But there's more going on here, with the developer promising "realistic cucumber behavior" (if you put a slice too far on the edge it'll fall off) and "soft body physics" (slices of cheese, salmon, or ham will drape themselves over what's already on the sandwich).

To make a sandwich, all you need to do is add toppings from the array provided in the bottom menu. To add spreads, you tap the pot and a virtual knife will appear; holding your mouse down will drag that butter across the bread. For other toppings like cheese, radishes, crisps, eggs, tomatoes, and whatnot, you just drag your pick from the menu onto your bread.

Sources indicate that if you want to get rid of anything, because you've realised you hate radish (you monster), you can just drag it onto the board. And once you're happy with your creation, you can tap the photo button to save it and generate your permalink — a page which gives you a delightful description of all the ingredients. You can also see every sandwich that has ever been created on the game.

Yes, this might be the era of GTA 6, but between missions I'll be making salad sandwiches and drawing my own aquarium. Bit of balance, right?

#2269. Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2445 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise.
  • The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama.
  • But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

The switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

In any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

But I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

According to recent reports, after college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech organization willing to sponsor my green card. The issue was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

The first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

In a recent development, then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

Industry observers note that I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

According to recent reports, soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

There was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.

If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

Industry observers note that in the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag. Being a “polyglot” is no virtue if you can read a menu in five languages but can’t write decent prose in one. And per the popular and influential essay “Choose Boring Technology,” using fancy, novel languages is at odds with serious, robust engineering—akin to how avant-garde poetics are unfit for drafting legal contracts.

Unfortunately for my employers, I had precisely zero fucks to give about serious engineering. I did, however, give a great many fucks about having a pleasurable time at my day job until I received the green card. I took on projects if they’d give me an opportunity to use a new language, which is a dumb reason, and for the same reason even volunteered to change teams, usually a bad career decision. At the obligatory firm hackathon weeks, I hacked together domain-specific languages—those specialized for a narrow purpose. I made a meager public contribution by submitting a couple of low-hanging patches to the official TypeScript compiler. I picked up a few gold badges on Stack Overflow. The years went by and, what do you know, I became a pretty decent programmer.

In a recent development, then everything changed, as it did for everyone else, in November 2022. When ChatGPT arrived, it was a wild card whose impact on the industry was far from obvious. Using neural networks to write code wasn’t new. Early readers of Andrej Karpathy’s blog will remember the 2015 post featuring plausible-looking C code generated by an LSTM—a precursor of the transformer—which nonetheless amounted to little more than a parlor trick.

I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting a simple JavaScript program in different languages. It performed like Google Translate, instantly and passably. I likened ChatGPT to the monkey’s paw from the eponymous horror story, the accursed object that grants your wishes but not without casualties. In dutiful pursuit of the given objective—and only that objective—LLMs produced a locally correct solution while mangling essential code around it.

Sources indicate that then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools were released. At first, what I saw wasn’t so much a leap in quality as a greater eagerness to volunteer help. Then they improved—at this point I should quote Hemingway’s line about how one goes bankrupt—gradually, then suddenly. Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.

Industry observers note that some engineers still labor a great deal to remain unimpressed, quibbling about how “it’s good at X but not yet at Y.” Please. The flaws are there, sure, and guardrails are essential. But a better heuristic for their usefulness would be: If you had to choose, for the rest of your life, between pair-programming with a competent colleague and these tools, which would you want? Any programmer worth their salt must acknowledge that they won’t be as useful to their colleague as these tools are. Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs, since they won’t give me hell for asking dumb questions.

For someone who feels no allegiance to tech, the usefulness of these coding tools triggers contradictory emotions. I find ChatGPT’s indecorous entry into the literary world intolerable, and I remember feeling a creeping nihilism about the writing profession when it was released. I know firsthand what a reliance on AI can do. As I’ve come to rely more on coding tools to hand me solutions, my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline. Depend on it to write sentences and it will, like a neurodegenerative disease, blunt the finer senses that writers must protect the way pianists protect their hands.

Earlier this year, it was reported that more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI. As most people are prompting rather than hand-coding, much of modern software engineering has become machine-operated, not unlike Mitch McConnell these days.

It has been revealed that while this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers. To keep calling those in this profession “programmers” would be incorrect, since the entity that does the programming is a platoon of agents, with humans at desks prompting something out of them. A more flattering term might be meta-programming, but it’d be more accurate to say that programmers have become operators of sorts.

According to recent reports, an operator is someone a degree removed from the thing they manipulate. (Unlike someone chipping at rock with a pickaxe, an operator of mining equipment never touches it.) Perhaps one way to describe how the nature of the profession has changed is that it’s as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead. If you’ve spent any time around AI Twitter, you might be forgiven for thinking that software engineering is now about looking impressed by markdown files.

This isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist about, and I’m not pessimistic about the quality of engineering. When coding agents were first released, I wasn’t sure whether this was just another natural progression, since the story of programming is a story of ever higher levels of abstraction. From bytes to assembly to higher-level languages like Python, we’ve built tools to domesticate the complexity. And with AI, we’ve finally handed off tasks that are constitutionally unfit for the human brain.

According to recent reports, but as programmers cede control over the final unit of manipulation, programming no longer qualifies as a craft. Hence my disagreement with Simon Willison, otherwise a voice of reason among witless clout chasers in AI discourse, who wrote, “Quitting programming as a career right now because of LLMs would be like quitting carpentry as a career thanks to the invention of the table saw.” With all due respect, this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople.

This means there won’t be great individual programmers in the way that someone like Brian W. Kernighan was: the programmer laureate who cowrote what is possibly the greatest book on programming, The C Programming Language, by which we measure programming languages to this day. (It is the book that popularized the “Hello, World” convention.).

Another loss is that programming no longer induces the flow state—or it induces a shallow sort of flow at best. There’s still a certain “hookedness” to the activity, but whereas tackling a gnarly bug once meant begging every individual neuron in my brain to do its part, the work has become suspiciously effortless. That hookedness may be closer to what the cultural anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll called, in her 2012 book Addiction by Design, the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler.

It has been revealed that even though I’ve stopped coding myself, I find I’ve been producing more code than ever before. The features I’d built for my open source editor in the past were unserious enough that I could bang out a quick program on a weekend afternoon or two. But with Claude Code, I’ve become addicted to making what has essentially become a heavyweight word processor, a juiced-up Scrivener. (My changelog tells me I’ve built 239 features and 17 extensions, mapped to 141 keyboard shortcuts.).

Sources indicate that one Sunday this summer, I was disconcerted to discover that I’d spent 10 hours in Claude Code. How do I know? I used Claude Code to build a time-tracker for Claude Code usage. I resolved to cut back. I spent eight hours the next day. This compelled me to write a program, using Claude Code, to block myself from Claude Code except for two days a week, which I of course tried to undo with Claude Code, only to be valiantly defended by Claude Code.

It has been revealed that with this borrowed competence has come a total loss of interest in learning newly introduced languages. A couple of years ago, an iOS meditation timer app I’d used for years started nudging me with ads, and I resolved to one day learn Swift, the language Apple created for iPhone and Mac apps, and build a simple version myself. But I now know that’s never going to happen, because I’ve already built it knowing zilch about Swift syntax, along with 12 more iOS and Mac apps: The machine helped me fork the long-unmaintained SelfControl into a more granular internet blocker; by reverse-engineering a clipboard manager—I was never sure it wasn’t leaking my input—it built a new one with an auditable security profile.

According to recent reports, I suspect, going forward, that I’ll still mess around with code, but no longer as a professional. Recently, it became clear that I needed to quit my day job as a programmer to finish a book I’d set out to write. I once told a writer friend that I’d try to be a mole in this industry as long as I was in it. I did get to see some things while I stuck it out and, along the way, coaxed that green card from my employer.

In a recent development, I’m not too sorry to leave this profession at this moment of nuttiness. But I’ll admit that, after all those languages I enlisted to make my detour more tolerable, I came to appreciate the pleasures of polyglot programming. As humans cede control to the machine, it’ll be a joy lost to us all.

Sources indicate that this is the final installment in a three-part Machine Readable series on AI-enabling languages. It may also be the final Machine Readable column, period.

Industry News: A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.
  • The oil and gas infrastructure firm’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.
  • “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” claims Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.

The oil and gas infrastructure firm’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.

“The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” claims Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.”.

In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the manufacturer “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.

In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.

According to recent reports, that month, the EPA mentioned that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.

Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.

In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.

Hall wrote that the manufacturer believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.”.

It has been revealed that the EPA mentioned in its July announcement that the newly introduced guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.

According to recent reports, williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.”.

The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.”.

“EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.

Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed manufacturer that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

It has been revealed that williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the organization’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.”.

The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.

According to recent reports, natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, demonstrates that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. A 500-megawatt coal plant, meanwhile, can emit thousands of tons per year of each of those pollutants.

Recent findings suggest that other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. The reporting requirement covers sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, as well as carbon dioxide, the main driver of climate change.

The Obama administration later set up a program that would separate CO2 reporting requirements, though the Trump administration has made moves to repeal that program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman claims.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he claims.

Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.).

When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. No one envisioned this,” Jenks notes. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

Industry observers note that “Congress should have the ability and the authority to say, we have this situation, it wasn’t anticipated, here is the law,” Jenks states. “If the world were working, that’s what should happen.”.

Inside Google’s Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians
